_readme: WORKSPACE CONFIGURATION. This is the live copy for this repository -- not a template. It sits
on the default branch as `.factory/config.json`, which is the only place and the only ref
either reader looks. The template it was copied from is `templates/factory-config.json` in
`yoselabs/factory-state`; see `templates/README.md` there for the full argument.
WHY JSON. Two readers have to agree on this file and neither may install anything:
`.github/workflows/signal-the-factory.yml` reads it in bash (jq, preinstalled on every hosted
runner) and `runner/allowlist.py` reads it in Python (`json`, stdlib, and `runner/*.py` is
stdlib-only on purpose). TOML would need `tomllib` on one side and a parser that does not
exist on the other; YAML needs a dependency on both. JSON is the only format both sides
already speak. Its one real cost is that it has no comment syntax, which is what this
`_readme` array is: prose, ignored by both readers, kept in the file because the file is what
an adopter opens.
WHY AN OBJECT AND NOT A LIST OF NAMES. This is workspace configuration generally. `users` is
one section of it; the next thing that is per-workspace policy rather than per-factory policy
gets its own key beside it, and neither reader has to change shape to allow that. `version`
is here so a future incompatible shape can be refused rather than misread -- both readers
check it.
WHO MAY QUEUE WORK. `users.allowed` is the complete list of GitHub logins whose issues and
issue comments this factory will act on. Everyone else may open issues and comment -- these
are public repositories and that is normal traffic -- and nothing they write becomes a work
item or spends a token. An EMPTY list, a MISSING file, or a file that does not parse means
NOBODY is allowed. Refuse-by-default, the same posture the branch allowlist in
`publish-workspace` takes.
WHICH COPY OF THIS FILE COUNTS. Only the one on the workspace's default branch, at its tip,
resolved when the check runs. Never the copy on a pull request branch, in a fork, or at any
ref carried in the event payload -- an allowlist a requester can edit in the same request is
not an allowlist. Both readers state how they pin this; see the comments there.
